content: Various versions of the circulating cathodic antigen (CCA) test were utilized in these studies. The review highlights the diagnostic specifications of tools used to detect Schistosoma infections in humans. While numerous point-of-care, molecular, and immunological methods show potential, no new diagnostic tool has been identified as clearly superior to the conventional methods currently in routine use. The population studied included adults and children (pre-school-aged and school-aged) living in endemic areas who had received elimination interventions. The diagnostic tools assessed included: 1. CCA v1 and v2: Circulating cathodic antigen urine cassette assays. 2. CAA: Circulating anodic antigen urine cassette assay. 3. FLOTAC: A stool-based diagnostic method. 4. SmCTF-RDT: Schistosoma mansoni cercarial transformation fluid rapid diagnostic test. 5. Sm DNA PCR: Detection of S. mansoni DNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). 6. SWAP ELISA: Soluble adult worm antigen preparation-specific IgG ELISA. 7. IgM ELISA: Detection of IgM antibodies against S. mansoni adult worm antigens. 8. IgG ELISA: Detection of IgG antibodies against S. mansoni adult worm antigens. 9. Anti-IgG RDT Sh: Anti-human IgG antibody rapid diagnostic test. 10. Proteinuria and Haematuria reagent strips: Used to detect proteinuria and haematuria as indirect markers of Schistosoma infection. 11. AWE-SEA ELISA: ELISA targeting S. mansoni adult worm extract and soluble egg antigen. 12. LAMP: Loop-mediated isothermal amplification for DNA detection. 13. IHA: Indirect hemagglutination assay. 14. Colorimetric test: Macroscopic detection of haematuria using a colorimetric method. 15. rSP13-ELISA: Recombinant protein-based ELISA kit. The comparator or reference tests included various Kato-Katz smear techniques (duplicate, triplicate, quadruplicate, sextuple) and urine filtration microscopy. Additionally, disease prevalence was assessed using both the reference and index tests. The findings revealed moderate certainty evidence (based on GRADE criteria) for most diagnostic tools. For example: CCA v1 showed sensitivity (Se) of 64–85% and specificity (Sp) of 62–66% compared to Kato-Katz. CCA v2 had Se of 46–59% and Sp of 87–88%. CAA demonstrated Se of 70–89% and Sp of 46–60%. FLOTAC showed improved sensitivity over time (65–93%) with specificity ranging from 61–70%. SmCTF-RDT had Se of 62–87% and Sp of 35–38%. Sm DNA PCR exhibited high sensitivity (96%) but low specificity (32%). SWAP ELISA had Se of 83% and Sp of 55%. IgM ELISA demonstrated high accuracy with Se of 92% and Sp of 91%. IgG ELISA had Se of 88% and Sp of 66%. Anti-IgG RDT Sh had low sensitivity (47%) and specificity (19%). Proteinuria and haematuria reagent strips showed Se of 72–86% and Sp of 86%. AWE-SEA ELISA had Se of 94% and Sp of 64%. LAMP demonstrated Se of 66–87% and Sp of 50–79%. IHA had Se of 81% and Sp of 7%. The colorimetric test had Se of 52% and Sp of 67%. rSP13-ELISA showed Se of 88% and Sp of 64%. The certainty of diagnostic accuracy estimates was limited due to the imperfections of the gold standard tests, leading to potential bias. Despite this, the estimates were considered sufficiently precise for most comparisons. The review also evaluated diagnostic tools for detecting Schistosoma in snails and environmental samples to verify transmission elimination. Conventional methods, such as direct shedding and snail crushing, were compared with molecular techniques like PCR, ELISA, and LAMP. Direct shedding involved isolating snails in water and visually observing the release of cercariae, while snail-crushing techniques used microscopy to detect cercariae. Molecular methods required laboratory infrastructure and expertise, with PCR and LAMP showing high sensitivity (93–100%). For non-human animal hosts, diagnostic tools included parasitological, immunological, and molecular techniques. Parasitological methods, such as Kato-Katz and miracidial hatching tests, had low sensitivity (23–27%) compared to PCR. Immunological assays, including ELISA and indirect hemagglutination, required serum samples and laboratory resources. Molecular tools like PCR demonstrated high sensitivity but required advanced infrastructure. The review emphasized the need for further development, validation, and standardization of diagnostic tools, particularly in field settings. It also highlighted the importance of addressing gaps in data, such as specificity estimates and the role of non-human hosts in transmission dynamics.
